We extracted several respiratory components from electrocardiography and photoplethysmography to investi-
gate respiratory drive mechanism. T ransfer function analysis was used to compare the derived respiration to
the reference respiration measured from nasal airﬂow to validate suitability of derived respiratory components.
Magnitude squared coherence estimate (MSCE) and phase spectrum were calculated to investigate the signif-
icance and phase difference, respectively . From the experiment, it was validated that every derived respiration
has high signiﬁcance (MSCE > 0.5) from the transfer analysis estimates. Moreover, phase difference, a time
relationship between respirations, showed that respiratory components have the sequential relationship.

1. INTRODUCTION
Cell, which composes human body, maintains its metabolism
from gas exchange and oxygen consumption. Respiration,
an activity to take oxygen from the outside air, inﬂuences on
physiological status. Blood serves to transport oxygen, more-
over cardiovascular signal depends on blood circulation. There-
fore, physiological signal, especially cardiovascular signal such
as electrocardiogram (ECG) and photoplethysmography (PPG) is
naturally affected on respiration. It has been demonstrated that
respiratory component could be derived from ECG and PPG.
Respiratory rhythm and depth are controlled by biophysi-
cal and biochemical processes in the central nervous system,
and these processes are inﬂuenced by and respond to changes
in O 2,C O 2 and hydrogen ion concentration. The exact mech-
anisms for these events have been studied in the past two
decades. It was suggested that central chemosensitive structures
can modify peripheral chemoreceptor responses by altering dis-
charges in parasympathetic and sympathetic nerves supplying
these receptors, and peripheral chemoreceptor drive can modu-
late central chemosensitivity during hypercapnia. More recently,
it was appeared that a number of neurotransmitters centrally
are involved in respiratory processes. Changes in CO 2 and O 2
tension also affect brain metabolism and hydrogen ion home-
ostasis and modify the central respiratory drive. It was showed

that the peripheral chemoreceptor causes the release of gluta-
mate to stimulate ventilation in the hypoxia condition. Central-
and peripheral-respiratory drive interconnection is described
in Figure 1.
From the previous studies, we supposed that peripheral res-
piratory drive precedes central respiratory drive, and they are
reﬂected by baseline, waveform amplitude and time intervals
of ECG and PPG. ECG is generated by only cardiac-induced
electrical activity which closely related on central respiratory
drive. However, PPG measures not only the cardiac-induced ﬂuc-
tuations but also cardiovascular changes such as sympathetic
changes in tissue blood volume. These characteristics could pro-
vide an evidence of peripheral respiratory drive.
It is well known fact that respiration could be derived from
ECG. Respiratory sinus rhythm (RSA), naturally occurring vari-
ation in heart rate that occurs during a respiratory cycle, is repre-
sentative example of ECG-derived respiration. Not only RSA, but
also amplitude variability of ECG (ECGV) derived respirations
were already compared and demonstrated. It was proposed that
ECG-derived respiration (EDR) based on the electrodes positions
is related on the heart movement, and transthoracic impedance
varies, as the lungs ﬁll and empty. ECG morphology analysis-
based methods were also proposed.
Respiration is generally located at 0.1 Hz to 0.5 Hz frequency
band, and in most cases respiratory components are reﬂected as
baseline changes of physiological waveform. Therefore, band-
pass ﬁltering-based baseline detection could be used for both

respiration derivations form ECG baseline (ECGBL) and respi-
ration derivation from PPG baseline (PPGBL).
PPG is composed with periodic pulse waves which are related
on pressure pulse. It was already shown that the heart rate vari-
ability (HRV) has the coincidence characteristics with pulse rate
variability (PRV). Considering of the periodic relevance between
pulse wave and ventricular contraction, ECG and PPG should
have a similar beat-to-beat characteristics. Amplitude of a pulse
wave is another important factor to reﬂect ventricular activity
and sympathetic nervous activity which is closely related on res-
piration. From these PPG characteristics, we could assume that
respiratory component could be derived from the features of PPG
waveform. Because PPG is controlled by hemodynamic property,
respiration which affects oxygen concentration is very important
factor to determine PPG waveform. Peak (upper inﬂection) and
foot (lower inﬂection) of PPG waveform is regarded as a homol-
ogous point of systolic and diastolic activity, respectively.
Derived respirations from ECG and PPG were compared with
reference respiration and analyzed by transfer function (TF)
analysis which is a frequently used technique in the assessment
of the relationship between short-term cardiovascular variability
signals, particularly blood pressure, heart rate and respiration.
From the TF analysis, we conﬁrm the coherences and the phase
difference, which means the signiﬁcance index and respiratory
sequence, respectively.
The aim of our study is summarized with the retrograde inves-
tigation of central and peripheral respiratory mechanism using
derived respirations from physiological characteristics of ECG
and PPG. This is the novel approach for the non-invasive retro-
grade study of respiratory drive mechanism, and it may provide
useful information to respiratory-related analysis.
2. METHODS
2.1. Subjects
Nine young and healthy subjects were participated in experiment,
and their age (mean ± SD) was 28.86 ± 2.91 years (range 26–35

years). There were no reported diseases and prescriptions of the
subjects. Prior to the experiment, the subjects were requested to
provide information about their physical condition. Every exper-
iment was performed in a typical biomedical laboratory at an
ambient room temperature from 11 am to 6 pm. Drinking and
smoking were prohibited during 24 hour and 2 hour before exper-
iment, respectively. Physical information and baseline values
in cardiovascular, ECG, ﬁnger PPG and respiration parameters
were also measured for demographical research (Table I).
2.2. Signal Measurement
ECG, PPG and respiration were simultaneously recorded for
comparative study. Forty-ﬁve dataset was obtained for simula-
tion. Experimental data was obtained in the sitting position with
spontaneous respiration. Every data has 1 minute length (sam-
pling frequency is 250 Hz). Signals were recorded by MP150
(BiopacTM, USA), and ECG 100C, PPG100C and SKT100C
modules were used for ECG, PPG and respiration measurement
respectively. ECG was recorded with LEAD II conﬁguration on
chest surface. PPG was measured on left index ﬁnger with TSD
100B plethysmograph transducer. TSD202 temperature probe
was also used for nasal airﬂow (NA) measurement. Arterial blood
pressure was measured by HEM-907 (Omron, Japan) before and
after experiment. For numerical simulation and statistical analy-
sis, MA TLAB (ver. 2008b, Mathworks, USA) was used.
2.3. Respiration Derivation
Respiration was derived by 8 different methods based on
the characteristic parameter of ECG and PPG. Characteristic
parameters depend on spatial- and temporal-values of ECG and
PPG. Figure 2 shows the graphical representation of the charac-
teristic parameters of ECG and PPG waveform.
Derivation method is summarized with baseline detection
method, beat-to-beat interval method and envelope detection
method. To detect baseline changes of ECG (ECGBL) and
PPG (PPGBL), bandpass ﬁlter which has respiratory passband

ration was calculated by R-to-R interval (RRI) which means
RSA in ECG and peak-to-peak or foot-to-foot interval of PPG.
Peak-to-peak interval and foot-to-foot interval of PPG respec-
tively mean the systolic pulse rate variability (SPRV) and dias-
tolic pulse wave variability (DPRV). Envelope-based respirations
were measured at the R-wave in ECG (ECGV) and at the peak
or foot in PPG. Peak envelope means the systolic PPG ampli-
tude variability (SPPGV) and foot envelope means diastolic PPG
amplitude variability (DPPGV).
PPG is composed with AC and DC component, and each com-
ponent means blood volume and baseline changing respectively.
In previous research, it was demonstrated that PPG DC com-
ponent is affected from respiration. Therefore, in both PPGV
conﬁgurations, we removed DC component by using 0.5 Hz
high pass ﬁlter to estimate AC component exactly. ECG baseline
wandering was also removed with the same method in ECGV
derivation.
Derived respiration has different time index according to the
derivation methods. In other words, derived signal is a tachome-
ter except on baseline-based respiration. Therefore, re-sampling
should be carried out to regulate non-uniform time index. Every
derived respiration was spline interpolated with 1 kHz sampling
rate, and then it was re-sampled with 7 Hz re-sampling frequency.
Figure 3 shows the derivation and regulation procedure for the
8 types of derived respiration.
To evaluate respiratory derivation performance, sensitivity
(SE), positive predictivity (+P) and detection rate (DR) were cal-
culated. SE means the proportion of actual positives which are
correctly identiﬁed, and it is calculated by Eq. (1). +P is the
proportion of event with positive test results which are correctly
classiﬁed, and it calculated Eq. (2). DR is a percentage for the
ratio of TP and total peaks. It could be calculated by Eq. (3).
